name: Chapter 5: Linear Inequalities
description: Inequalities, rules for solving, number-line graphs, double inequalities, systems, word problems, modulus and quadratic inequalities, half-planes.

cards.term: Define an inequality.
cards.definition: Two real numbers or algebraic expressions related by <, >, ≤ or ≥

cards.term: Numerical, literal and double inequalities: one example each?
cards.definition: Numerical: 3 < 5. Literal: x ≥ 3. Double: 3 < x < 5 (x is between 3 and 5)

cards.term: Strict vs slack inequalities?
cards.definition: Strict: < and > (endpoint excluded). Slack (non-strict): ≤ and ≥ (endpoint included)

cards.term: When is ax + b < 0 a linear inequality in one variable?
cards.definition: When a ≠ 0. In two variables, ax + by < c with a ≠ 0, b ≠ 0

cards.term: Is ax² + bx + c ≤ 0 linear?
cards.definition: No: it is a quadratic inequality in one variable (a ≠ 0)

cards.term: Ravi has ₹200 and buys x packets of rice at ₹30 each (whole packets only). Write the inequality.
cards.definition: 30x < 200: he cannot spend exactly ₹200 with whole packets, so the spending is strictly less

cards.term: Reshma has ₹120; registers cost ₹40, pens ₹20. Write the inequality for x registers and y pens.
cards.definition: 40x + 20y ≤ 120, which combines 40x + 20y < 120 (inequality) and 40x + 20y = 120 (equation)

cards.term: What is a solution and a solution set of an inequality?
cards.definition: A value of the variable that makes it a true statement; the solution set is all such values. E.g. 30x < 200 (whole numbers): {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}

cards.term: Rule 1 for solving inequalities?
cards.definition: Add or subtract the same number on both sides: the sign is unchanged

cards.term: Rule 2 for solving inequalities?
cards.definition: Multiply or divide both sides by the same positive number: sign unchanged. By a negative number: reverse the sign (< ↔ >, ≤ ↔ ≥)

cards.term: Why does multiplying by a negative reverse the inequality? Examples?
Multiplying by a negative number reverses the inequality
cards.definition: Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number mirrors the number line, so the inequality sign reverses: 2<3 gives −2>−3

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Reversing the sign · intuition

Multiply both sides of 2 < 3 by −1. Which way does the inequality go, and why?

Where do 2 and 3 land after the mirror?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Reversing the sign · intuition

Multiply both sides of 2 < 3 by −1. Which way does the inequality go, and why?

Multiplying by −1 mirrors the number line about 0: 2 → −2 and 3 → −3. The larger number is now on the left, so < becomes >: −2 > −3.

Rule: multiply or divide by a negative → flip the sign. By a positive → no change.

cards.term: Trap: solve −2x < 4.
cards.definition: Divide by −2 and flip: x > −2. Forgetting the flip is the most common mistake

cards.term: Trap: if 0 < a < b, compare 1/a and 1/b.
cards.definition: 1/a > 1/b. Taking reciprocals of positive numbers reverses the order (1/2 > 1/3). If a < 0 < b, then 1/a < 1/b

cards.term: Can you square both sides of an inequality?
cards.definition: Only when both sides are non-negative. −3 < 2 but (−3)² = 9 > 4. Safe form: a² < b² ⟺ |a| < |b|

cards.term: Trap: solve (x + 1)/(x − 2) ≥ 0 by cross-multiplying?
cards.definition: Never multiply by an expression of unknown sign. Use signs instead: the answer is x ≤ −1 or x > 2 (the point 2 is excluded because it makes the denominator 0)

cards.term: Example 1: solve 30x < 200 for (i) natural x, (ii) integer x.
Ex 5.1 Q1: solve 24x < 100 for natural and integer x.
cards.definition: x < 25/6 ≈ 4.17: natural {1, 2, 3, 4}; integers {…, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4}

cards.term: Ex 5.1 Q2: solve −12x > 30 for natural and integer x.
cards.definition: Divide by −12 and flip: x < −5/2. Natural: no solution (φ); integers: {…, −4, −3}

cards.term: Example 2: solve 5x − 3 < 3x + 1 for (i) integer x, (ii) real x.
cards.definition: 2x < 4 → x < 2. (i) {…, −1, 0, 1} (ii) (−∞, 2)

cards.term: Example 3: solve 4x + 3 < 6x + 7.
cards.definition: −2x < 4 → x > −2: (−2, ∞)

cards.term: Example 4: solve (5 − 2x)/3 ≤ x/6 − 5.
cards.definition: Multiply by 6: 2(5 − 2x) ≤ x − 30 → 10 − 4x ≤ x − 30 → −5x ≤ −40 → x ≥ 8, i.e. [8, ∞)

cards.term: Method: solving a linear inequality with fractions.
cards.definition: 1) Multiply by the LCD (positive) to clear fractions. 2) Expand brackets. 3) Collect x on one side. 4) Divide by its coefficient, flipping if negative. 5) Write the answer as an interval
x > −4; x < −3; x ≤ −3; x ≤ 4
4x + 6 − 10 < 6x − 12 → −4 + 12 < 2x → x > 4
32 − 3x > x + 24 → 8 > 4x → x < 2

cards.term: Number line: how do you graph x < a and x > a?
cards.definition: Open circle at a (a excluded), thick line to the left for x < a, to the right for x > a

cards.term: Number line: how do you graph x ≤ a and x ≥ a?
cards.definition: Filled circle at a (a included), thick line to the left (≤) or right (≥)

cards.term: Example 5: graph of x < 3
cards.definition: 7x+3<5x+9 gives x<3; open circle at 3 with the ray to the left

Example 5: solve 7x + 3 < 5x + 9 and graph the solution.

2x < 6 → x < 3, i.e. (−∞, 3). Open circle at 3, ray to the left.

cards.term: Example 6: graph of x ≥ 1
cards.definition: (3x−4)/2 ≥ (x+1)/4 − 1 gives x ≥ 1; filled circle at 1 with the ray to the right

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Inequalities · number line

Example 6: solve (3x − 4)/2 ≥ (x + 1)/4 − 1 and graph the solution.

Solve first, then mark the endpoints.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Inequalities · number line

Example 6: solve (3x − 4)/2 ≥ (x + 1)/4 − 1 and graph the solution.

Multiply by 4: 2(3x − 4) ≥ x − 3 → 6x − 8 ≥ x − 3 → 5x ≥ 5 → x ≥ 1, i.e. [1, ∞). Filled circle at 1, ray to the right.

cards.definition: x < 3; x > −1; 3 − 3x < 2x + 8 → x > −1

cards.term: Method: translating a word problem into an inequality.
cards.definition: Let x be the unknown. Translate: “at least” → ≥, “at most / not more than” → ≤, “more than” → >, “less than” → <. Solve, then interpret (integers? natural numbers?)

cards.term: Example 7: marks 62 and 48 in two terms. Minimum marks in the annual exam for an average of at least 60?
Ex 5.1 Q21: Ravi scored 70 and 75. Minimum in the third test for an average of at least 60?
cards.definition: (145 + x)/3 ≥ 60 → x ≥ 35

cards.term: Ex 5.1 Q22: Sunita has 87, 92, 94, 95. Minimum in the fifth exam to average at least 90?
Example 8: pairs of consecutive odd naturals, both larger than 10, sum less than 40?
Ex 5.1 Q23: consecutive odd positive integers, both smaller than 10, sum more than 11?
cards.definition: x + 2 < 10 and 2x + 2 > 11 → 4.5 < x < 8, x odd: (5, 7) and (7, 9)

cards.term: Ex 5.1 Q24: consecutive even positive integers, both larger than 5, sum less than 23?
Ex 5.1 Q25: longest side = 3 × shortest, third side = longest − 2. Perimeter ≥ 61. Minimum shortest side?
cards.definition: x + 3x + (3x − 2) ≥ 61 → 7x ≥ 63 → x ≥ 9 cm

cards.term: Ex 5.1 Q26: board of 91 cm cut into x, x + 3, 2x; the third must be at least 5 cm longer than the second. Range of x?
Method: solve a double inequality like a ≤ f(x) < b.
cards.definition: Apply every operation to all three parts at once (add, multiply, flip if negative), leaving x alone in the middle

cards.term: Example 9: solve −8 ≤ 5x − 3 < 7.
cards.definition: −5 ≤ 5x < 10 → −1 ≤ x < 2

cards.term: Example 10: solve −5 ≤ (5 − 3x)/2 ≤ 8.
cards.definition: −10 ≤ 5 − 3x ≤ 16 → −15 ≤ −3x ≤ 11 → divide by −3 (flip both):\[-11/3 \le x \le 5\]

cards.term: Trap: after dividing a double inequality by a negative number, what changes?
cards.definition: Both signs flip and the two end values swap places: −15 ≤ −3x ≤ 11 becomes 5 ≥ x ≥ −11/3, written −11/3 ≤ x ≤ 5

cards.term: Misc Q1 and Q2: solve 2 ≤ 3x − 4 ≤ 5 and 6 ≤ −3(2x − 4) < 12.
cards.definition: 6 ≤ 3x ≤ 9 → [2, 3]. Second: 6 ≤ −6x + 12 < 12 → −6 ≤ −6x < 0 → 0 < x ≤ 1

cards.term: Method: solving a system of inequalities in one variable.
cards.definition: Solve each inequality separately, graph both on one number line, and take the overlap (intersection) of the solution sets

cards.term: Example 11: solve 3x − 7 < 5 + x and 11 − 5x ≤ 1.
cards.definition: x < 6 and x ≥ 2 → common part [2, 6)

cards.term: Example 11: system solution on the number line
cards.definition: 3x−7<5+x gives x<6; 11−5x≤1 gives x≥2; the common part is 2≤x<6

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Inequalities · number line

Example 11: show the solution of {3x − 7 < 5 + x, 11 − 5x ≤ 1} on the number line.

Solve first, then mark the endpoints.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Inequalities · number line

Example 11: show the solution of {3x − 7 < 5 + x, 11 − 5x ≤ 1} on the number line.

x < 6 and x ≥ 2. The bold stretch where both hold: 2 ≤ x < 6.

cards.term: Misc Q7: solve 5x + 1 > −24 and 5x − 1 < 24.
cards.definition: x > −5 and x < 5 → (−5, 5)

cards.term: Misc Q8: solve 2(x − 1) < x + 5 and 3(x + 2) > 2 − x.
cards.definition: x < 7 and x > −1 → (−1, 7)

cards.term: Misc Q9: solve 3x − 7 > 2(x − 6) and 6 − x > 11 − 2x.
cards.definition: x > −5 and x > 5 → the overlap is (5, ∞)

cards.term: When is the solution of a system empty?
cards.definition: When the individual solution sets do not overlap, e.g. x > 5 and x < 2

cards.term: Example 12: acid to be kept between 30°C and 35°C. Range in °F using C = (5/9)(F − 32)?
Misc Q11: solution between 68°F and 77°F. Range in °C (F = 9C/5 + 32)?

Method: mixture problems with percentages.
cards.definition:
Write “acid in mixture = acid from each part”, and “total acid ÷ total volume” between the two limits
clear the decimals with the LCD
solve the double inequality

cards.term: Misc Q12: 640 L of 8% boric acid; add x L of 2% so that the mixture is between 4% and 6%. Range of x?
Misc Q13: 1125 L of 45% acid; how much water must be added for between 25% and 30% acid?
Misc Q14: IQ = (MA/CA) × 100, children of age 12, 80 ≤ IQ ≤ 140. Range of MA?
|x − a| < r as a distance band
cards.definition: |x−a|<r means a−r<x<a+r (within distance r of a); |x−a|>r means x<a−r or x>a+r; |x−3|<2 gives (1,5)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Modulus inequalities · intuition

Solve |x − 3| < 2 by reading it as a distance.

Read |x − a| as the distance between x and a.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Modulus inequalities · intuition

Solve |x − 3| < 2 by reading it as a distance.

|x − 3| is the distance from x to 3. “Distance < 2” means x lies within 2 of 3: 1 < x < 5.

|x − a| < r ⟺ a − r < x < a + r (one band, AND).
|x − a| > r ⟺ x < a − r or x > a + r (two outer rays, OR).

cards.term: Modulus inequalities
cards.definition: |x| < r: −r < x < r; |x| ≤ r: −r ≤ x ≤ r; |x| > r: x  r; |x| ≥ r: x ≤ −r or x ≥ r; |x − a| < r: a − r < x < a + r; |x| < negative number: no solution

cards.term: Solve |2x − 3| ≤ 5.
Solve |x + 1| ≥ 3.
cards.definition: x + 1 ≤ −3 or x + 1 ≥ 3 → x ≤ −4 or x ≥ 2

cards.term: Number line for |x − 1| ≥ 2
cards.definition: |x−1|≥2 gives x≤−1 or x≥3: two rays, endpoints included

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Modulus · number line

Show the solution of |x − 1| ≥ 2 on the number line.

Solve first, then mark the endpoints.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Modulus · number line

Show the solution of |x − 1| ≥ 2 on the number line.

|x − 1| ≥ 2 → x − 1 ≤ −2 or x − 1 ≥ 2 → x ≤ −1 or x ≥ 3: two outer rays (a union).

cards.term: Triangle inequality for real numbers?
cards.definition: |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|; equality iff ab ≥ 0. Also |a − b| ≥ ||a| − |b||

cards.term: Trap: solving |x| < 3 as x < 3 only, or |x| > 3 as −3 < x?
cards.definition: Both wrong. |x| < 3 is a band (AND): −3 < x < 3. |x| > 3 is two rays (OR): x < −3 or x > 3

cards.term: (x − a)(x − b) < 0 with a < b: solution?
cards.definition: a < x < b (between the roots). And (x − a)(x − b) > 0: x < a or x > b (outside the roots)

cards.term: Solve x² − 5x + 6 < 0.
cards.definition: (x − 2)(x − 3) < 0 → 2 < x < 3

cards.term: Solve x² − 5x + 6 > 0.
cards.definition: x < 2 or x > 3 (outside the roots)

cards.term: Solve x² − 4 ≥ 0 and x² ≤ 9.
cards.definition: x² ≥ 4 → x ≤ −2 or x ≥ 2. x² ≤ 9 → −3 ≤ x ≤ 3

cards.term: Solve x² + x + 1 > 0.
cards.definition: D = 1 − 4 < 0 and a > 0, so the parabola is always above the axis: all real x. If D < 0: ax² + bx + c has the sign of a for every x

cards.term: Solve a polynomial inequality by the wavy-curve method
cards.definition: (x−1)(x−2)(x−4) ≤ 0: signs alternate +,−,+,− from the right across simple roots; solution (−∞,1] ∪ [2,4]; repeated roots do not flip the sign

cards.term: Method: solve a rational inequality such as (x + 1)/(x − 2) ≥ 0.
cards.definition: Critical points = zeros of numerator and denominator (−1, 2). Sign chart: + on the far right, alternate. Include numerator zeros only if ≥ or ≤; always exclude denominator zeros. Answer: (−∞, −1] ∪ (2, ∞)
Critical points −2, 3; the quotient is negative between them: −2 < x < 3

cards.term: AM–GM for positive numbers: x + 1/x ≥ ?
cards.definition: 2 for x > 0, with equality at x = 1. For x < 0, x + 1/x ≤ −2

cards.term: a > 0, b > 0: compare (a + b)/2 and √(ab).
cards.definition: (a + b)/2 ≥ √(ab) (AM ≥ GM), equality iff a = b. Proof: (√a − √b)² ≥ 0

cards.term: Beyond the textbook text: how do you graph ax + by ≤ c?
cards.definition: 1) Draw the line ax + by = c (solid for ≤ ≥, dashed for < >). 2) Test a point, usually the origin. 3) Shade the side that satisfies it

cards.term: Graph a linear inequality in two variables (test-point method)
cards.definition: Draw the boundary line (solid for ≤ ≥, dashed for < >), then shade the side containing a test point that satisfies the inequality, e.g. origin for 2x+3y≤6

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Two variables · half-plane · beyond the textbook

Represent 2x + 3y ≤ 6 on the plane. How do you decide which side to shade?

Find where the boundary line cuts the axes.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Two variables · half-plane · beyond the textbook

Represent 2x + 3y ≤ 6 on the plane. How do you decide which side to shade?

1) Draw the line 2x + 3y = 6 through (3, 0) and (0, 2). Solid for ≤ or ≥; dashed for < or >.

2) Test the origin: 0 ≤ 6 is true → shade the side containing (0, 0). (If the line passes through the origin, test another point.)

cards.term: Solution region of a system of linear inequalities
cards.definition: The solution of a system is the common part of the half-planes; x+y≤4, x≥1, y≥0 gives the triangle (1,0),(4,0),(1,3) (feasible region)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
System of inequalities · beyond the textbook

Show the solution region of x + y ≤ 4, x ≥ 1 and y ≥ 0.

Shade each half-plane; keep the overlap.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
System of inequalities · beyond the textbook

Show the solution region of x + y ≤ 4, x ≥ 1 and y ≥ 0.

The solution of a system is the overlap of all the half-planes: here the triangle with corners (1, 0), (4, 0), (1, 3).

Corner points come from pairs of boundary lines. (This is exactly the feasible region of linear programming in Class 12.)

cards.term: Which half-plane is x + y > 5 (test the origin)?
cards.definition: 0 + 0 > 5 is false, so shade the side not containing the origin, with a dashed line

cards.term: What does x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 mean geometrically?
cards.definition: The first quadrant (including both axes)

cards.term: Vertices of the region 2x + y ≤ 8, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0?
cards.definition: (0, 0), (4, 0), (0, 8): intercepts of 2x + y = 8 and the axes

cards.term:
MCQ: The solution of 3x − 7 > 5x − 1 is
(a) x > −3 (b) x < −3 (c) x > 3 (d) x < 3
cards.definition: (b): −6 > 2x → x < −3
−3x < −30 → x > 10: (a)

cards.term:
MCQ: The solution set of |x − 2| < 3 is
(a) (−1, 5) (b) [−1, 5] (c) (−5, 1) (d) (5, ∞)
cards.definition: (a): −3 < x − 2 < 3

cards.term: Integer answer (JEE Main): the number of integers x with −5 < 2x + 1 < 9?

MCQ: The number of positive integers satisfying x² − 5x + 6 ≤ 0 is
(a) 1 (b) 2 (c) 3 (d) 0
cards.definition: 2 ≤ x ≤ 3 → 2 and 3: (b) 2
Positive outside the roots −2 and 1 (both excluded): (b)

cards.term:
Assertion–Reason.
A: If a > b then ac > bc.
R: Multiplying an inequality by a negative number reverses it.
(a) Both true, R explains A (b) Both true, R does not explain A (c) A false, R true (d) Both false
cards.definition: (c): A is false when c < 0 (or 0); R is the correct rule

cards.term:
Assertion–Reason.
A: The solution of x² + 1 < 0 is φ.
R: x² + 1 ≥ 1 for all real x.
(a) Both true, R explains A (b) Both true, R does not explain A (c) A true, R false (d) A false, R true
cards.definition: (a)

cards.term: True/False (2 marks): if x < y and z < 0 then xz < yz.
cards.definition: False: multiplying by a negative z reverses it, so xz > yz

cards.term: 2-mark: solve 2(x − 1) < x + 5 and represent the solution on the number line.
cards.definition: x < 7: (−∞, 7), open circle at 7 with the ray to the left

cards.term: 3-mark: solve −4 ≤ (3 − 2x)/5 < 1 and list the integral solutions.
Case-based: a phone plan costs ₹200 + ₹1.5 per minute. Budget is at most ₹500. How many whole minutes can be used?
cards.definition: 200 + 1.5x ≤ 500 → x ≤ 200: at most 200 minutes

cards.term: Case-based: a fence needs a perimeter of at least 60 m for a rectangle whose length is 2 m more than its width w. Find w.
cards.definition: 2(w + w + 2) ≥ 60 → 4w + 4 ≥ 60 → w ≥ 14 m
